lead: This unit is about direct-current circuits: what the three basic elements do, how sources drive them, and the laws and theorems that reduce any network to a few numbers. After it you can read a circuit diagram, write the smallest set of equations for it, and replace a tangle of resistors with one source and one resistance.
about: DC Circuits and Network Theorems begins with the three lumped elements — resistance, inductance and capacitance (1.1) — and the sources that drive them (1.2). Ohm's law and Kirchhoff's laws (1.3) supply the two conservation rules every later method rests on. Chapter 1.4 reduces series-parallel networks and gives the divider rules, and 1.5 adds source transformation and star-delta for networks that refuse to reduce. Mesh and node analysis (1.6) turn any circuit into a small set of equations you can solve. The last three chapters are the network theorems: superposition (1.7), Thevenin and Norton (1.8), and maximum power transfer (1.9). Each theorem is a shortcut that reuses the reduction and equation skills built earlier.

chapters.idea: Resistance, inductance and capacitance are the three lumped elements, and each is completely described by one fixed relation between its voltage and its current.
chapters.depth: Define charge (Q, coulomb), current (I = dQ/dt, ampere), voltage (V, volt, energy per coulomb), power (P = VI, watt) and energy (joule). Ideal resistor: v = iR, R in ohm, power P = i²R = v²/R, no energy stored. Ideal inductor: v = L di/dt, L in henry, stores ½Li², and behaves as a short circuit in DC steady state. Ideal capacitor: i = C dv/dt, C in farad, stores ½Cv², and behaves as an open circuit in DC steady state. Classify elements as linear or non-linear, active or passive, lumped or distributed — only a few universities teach the lumped/distributed distinction formally. Give one real example per element: heater coil, transformer winding, capacitor inside a fan regulator. Give the v-i relation for each element as a small table in the text.

figure.title: v-i relation decides DC behaviour
figure.aria: Three element blocks — resistor, inductor, capacitor — each pointing down to the same DC steady-state block, labelled no change, short and open.

chapters.example: A 10 V DC source feeds a 5 Ω resistor in series with one unknown element. After a long time, find the current, the voltage across the element and the energy stored, when the element is (a) a 5 Ω resistor, (b) a 2 H inductor, (c) a 2 mF capacitor. Answers: (a) total 10 Ω, I = 1 A, 1 V? no — 5 V across each, P = 5 W each, energy 0; (b) inductor is a short, I = 10/5 = 2 A, element voltage 0 V, stored energy ½Li² = ½ × 2 × 4 = 4 J; (c) capacitor is an open, I = 0 A, element voltage 10 V, stored energy ½CV² = ½ × 2×10⁻³ × 100 = 0.1 J.
chapters.trap: Swapping the DC steady-state behaviour: the inductor becomes a short circuit (not an open) and the capacitor becomes an open circuit (not a short) after a long time.
chapters.leave: Electrostatics, magnetic flux, reluctance and Faraday's law to Unit 3; transient growth and decay of L and C currents to a later study; AC impedance and phasors to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: An ideal source holds its voltage or its current whatever the load, and a dependent source holds it in a fixed ratio to some other voltage or current in the circuit.
chapters.depth: Ideal voltage source: fixed V, internal resistance zero, drawn as a circle with + and −. Ideal current source: fixed I, internal resistance infinite, drawn as a circle with an arrow showing the direction of current inside the source. Practical source: ideal source plus internal resistance, so terminal voltage falls as load current rises. Independent sources set their own value; dependent (controlled) sources take a value from another branch. Cover the four types with gain symbols: VCVS with μ (V/V), VCCS with g (siemens), CCVS with r (ohm), CCCS with β (A/A). Combination of sources: voltage sources in series add, current sources in parallel add, and sources in parallel/series must be equal to combine. Some syllabi word this as 'types of DC sources' and 'combination of DC sources'.

figure.aria: A hierarchy splitting sources into independent voltage and current sources, and dependent sources into VCVS, VCCS, CCVS and CCCS.

chapters.example: A 5 Ω resistor carries 3 A. A voltage-controlled voltage source of gain μ = 4 senses the voltage across this resistor and drives a 10 Ω load. Find the controlling voltage, the source output voltage, the load current and the power delivered to the load. Answers: controlling voltage = 3 × 5 = 15 V; output = 4 × 15 = 60 V; load current = 60/10 = 6 A; load power = 60 × 6 = 360 W.
chapters.trap: Treating a dependent source like an independent one: it can never be 'switched off' on its own, only the voltage or current that controls it can be set to zero.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.1 for the v-i relation of the resistor that provides the controlling voltage or current.
chapters.leave: Turning a practical voltage source into a current source to chapter 1.5; the role of dependent sources inside Thevenin equivalents to chapter 1.8.

chapters.idea: Ohm's law fixes the voltage-current relation inside a resistor, while Kirchhoff's current law conserves charge at a node and Kirchhoff's voltage law conserves energy round a loop.
chapters.depth: State Ohm's law and its limits: linear, bilateral, constant temperature, so it fails for lamps and thermistors. KCL: the sum of currents entering a node equals the sum leaving, or Σ I = 0 with all arrows leaving. KVL: the algebraic sum of voltages round any closed loop is zero, a rise counted negative if a drop is positive. Derive the series and parallel rules from KVL and KCL, not as separate facts. Count independent equations: n − 1 current equations at n nodes, b − n + 1 voltage equations for b branches. Show the power balance check: total power delivered by sources equals total power absorbed by elements.

figure.title: Solving any DC circuit
figure.aria: A four-step flow: assign current directions, write KCL and KVL equations, solve them, then check the power balance.

chapters.example: A 20 V DC source drives 2 Ω, 3 Ω and 5 Ω in series. Find the current, the voltage across each resistor, and verify both KVL and power balance. Answers: R_total = 10 Ω, I = 2 A; voltages 4 V, 6 V and 10 V, which add to 20 V; power supplied = 20 × 2 = 40 W; power absorbed = 4×2 + 9×2 + 25×2 = 8 + 18 + 50? no — i²R gives 4×2 = 8 W, 4×3 = 12 W, 4×5 = 20 W, total 40 W, equal to the supplied power.
chapters.trap: Sign slips in KVL: writing every term as a drop even when the loop passes through a source from − to +, which is a rise.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 1.1 and 1.2 for element relations and source symbols.
chapters.leave: Systematic multi-loop equation writing to chapter 1.6; the sinusoidal version of these laws to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Reduce the network step by step to one resistance to get the total current, then walk back with the voltage divider and current divider rules to get the branch quantity asked for.
chapters.depth: Series: same current, R = R1 + R2 + …, voltage divides. Parallel: same voltage, 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + …, and the two-resistor form R1R2/(R1+R2), current divides. Voltage divider V1 = V × R1/(R1 + R2); current divider I1 = I × R2/(R1 + R2), the other resistor on top. Extend the same rules to inductors (series and parallel like resistors) and capacitors (series and parallel the opposite way). Treat ladder networks and the effect of an open or short branch. Some syllabi call this 'network reduction techniques'.

figure.title: Reducing a network step by step
figure.aria: A four-step reduction of one network: the parallel pair becomes 4 Ω, the series total becomes 10 Ω, and the source current becomes 2.4 A.

chapters.example: A 24 V source feeds R1 = 4 Ω in series with the parallel pair R2 = 12 Ω and R3 = 6 Ω, then R4 = 2 Ω back to the source. Find the total resistance, the source current, the voltage across the parallel pair, and the current in each of R2 and R3. Answers: 12 ∥ 6 = 4 Ω; R_total = 4 + 4 + 2 = 10 Ω; I = 2.4 A; pair voltage = 2.4 × 4 = 9.6 V; I_R2 = 9.6/12 = 0.8 A and I_R3 = 9.6/6 = 1.6 A, which add to 2.4 A.
chapters.trap: Using R1/(R1 + R2) in the current divider. The current divider puts the other resistance on top: I1 = I × R2/(R1 + R2).
chapters.prereq: Chapters 1.1 and 1.3 for element values and for the KVL and KCL proofs of the rules.
chapters.leave: Networks that are neither series nor parallel, such as a bridge, to chapter 1.5; multi-source reduction to chapters 1.6 and 1.7.

chapters.idea: A practical voltage source and a practical current source are the same source seen from the terminals, and a star of three resistors is the same three-terminal network as a delta, so either can be swapped for an easier circuit.
chapters.depth: Source transformation: V_s in series with R becomes I_s = V_s/R in parallel with the same R, and back with V_s = I_s R. The arrow of the current source points from − to + inside the source. Only practical sources transform; an ideal voltage source (R = 0) or ideal current source (R = ∞) has no partner. Star-delta: name the star arms R_a, R_b, R_c and the delta sides R_ab, R_bc, R_ca. Delta to star, R_a = R_ab R_ca/(R_ab + R_bc + R_ca). Star to delta, R_ab = (R_a R_b + R_b R_c + R_c R_a)/R_c. Balanced case: R_delta = 3 R_star. Use these when the network is a bridge and cannot be reduced by series-parallel rules.

figure.title: Two-way source transformation
figure.aria: Two blocks, a voltage source with a series resistance and a current source with a parallel resistance, joined by arrows in both directions with the conversion formulas.

chapters.example: A 12 V source in series with 6 Ω feeds a 3 Ω load. Convert the source, then find the load current from the converted circuit. Also convert a star of three 9 Ω resistors into its delta. Answers: converted source is 2 A in parallel with 6 Ω; 6 ∥ 3 = 2 Ω and the divider gives I_load = 2 × 6/(6 + 3) = 1.333 A, which matches 12/9 = 1.333 A in the original circuit; balanced star to delta gives 3 × 9 = 27 Ω on each side.
chapters.trap: Reversing the current source arrow, or trying to transform an ideal source that has no series or parallel resistance.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.2 for source types and chapter 1.4 for series-parallel reduction.
chapters.leave: Using transformations to build Thevenin equivalents, including dependent-source cases, to chapter 1.8; the AC impedance version to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Mesh analysis writes KVL round the independent loops using mesh currents, and node analysis writes KCL at the independent nodes using node voltages; both give the minimum set of equations for any circuit.
chapters.depth: Mesh: draw one current per window, all clockwise; self resistance times own mesh current, minus shared resistance times neighbour mesh current, equals the source sum driving that mesh. A current source shared by two meshes needs a supermesh; a current source on the outer edge fixes one mesh current directly. Node: pick a reference node at 0 V, write KCL at each other node as Σ (V_node − V_neighbour)/R = source currents entering; a voltage source between two non-reference nodes needs a supernode. Count the unknowns and pick the method with fewer equations. Show the matrix form and solve by substitution or Cramer's rule. Some syllabi say 'nodal voltage analysis'.

figure.title: Mesh equations in matrix form
figure.aria: A coefficient array with rows for mesh 1 and mesh 2: 6, −4, 8 and −4, 10, 2, where the shared 4 Ω terms are the off-diagonal entries.

chapters.example: Two meshes share a 4 Ω resistor. Mesh 1 also has an 8 V source and a 2 Ω resistor; mesh 2 also has a 2 V source and a 6 Ω resistor, and both sources drive current clockwise. Find i1, i2 and the current in the shared resistor. Answers: 6 i1 − 4 i2 = 8 and −4 i1 + 10 i2 = 2, giving i1 = 2 A and i2 = 1 A; the shared resistor carries i1 − i2 = 1 A from mesh 1 side to mesh 2 side.
chapters.trap: Getting the sign of the shared resistance term wrong, and forgetting the supermesh or supernode when a source sits between two meshes or two nodes.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 1.3 and 1.4 for KVL, KCL and series-parallel reduction.
chapters.leave: Using these equations to prove the theorems to chapters 1.7 and 1.8; the phasor version for R-L-C circuits to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: In a linear circuit with several independent sources, the voltage or current anywhere is the sum of the values produced by each source acting alone.
chapters.depth: Statement and the two conditions: the circuit must be linear and the elements bilateral. Procedure: keep one independent source, replace every other voltage source by a short circuit and every other current source by an open circuit, solve, repeat for each source, then add with signs. Dependent sources stay in place every time, because they are part of the circuit, not a driving source. Superposition applies to voltage and current, never to power, since power goes as the square of current. Show a check against a single nodal equation.

figure.title: Superposition in three steps
figure.aria: The full two-source circuit splits into a sub-circuit with only the 12 V source and one with only the 3 A source, each giving 1.2 A, which are added at the end.

chapters.example: A 12 V source with 4 Ω in series feeds node A. A 3 A current source injects current into node A, and a 6 Ω resistor connects A to ground. Use superposition to find the current in the 6 Ω resistor and the voltage at A. Answers: with only the 12 V source, I = 12/10 = 1.2 A; with only the 3 A source, the divider gives 3 × 4/(4 + 6) = 1.2 A; total 2.4 A, so V_A = 2.4 × 6 = 14.4 V, matching the nodal equation (V − 12)/4 + V/6 = 3.
chapters.trap: Applying superposition to power, and switching off a dependent source as if it were independent.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 1.2, 1.3 and 1.6 for source types, the basic laws and one reliable solution method.
chapters.leave: Collapsing the whole network into one source, which is Thevenin's job, to chapter 1.8; the reciprocity theorem, taught in a few universities, is a cousin of this idea and is not needed here.

chapters.idea: Any linear two-terminal network behaves, as far as the load is concerned, like one voltage source V_th in series with one resistance R_th, or the same resistance in parallel with one current source I_N.
chapters.depth: Thevenin: remove the load, find the open-circuit voltage V_th across the terminals, then kill all independent sources and find the resistance R_th looking in. Norton: the same R_N = R_th with the short-circuit current I_N = V_th/R_th. Draw both equivalents and check the load line. With dependent sources present, R_th cannot be found by killing sources alone: apply a test source (1 V or 1 A), measure the other quantity, and use R_th = V_test/I_test, with all independent sources killed. Use the equivalent to find the load current quickly when only the load changes, and to cascade stages. Some syllabi also put the reciprocity theorem and Tellegen's theorem in this slot; only a few universities teach them, so one line each is enough.

figure.title: Thevenin view of a network
figure.aria: A linear network is replaced by a 4 V source in series with 2 Ω, which then drives a 2 Ω load carrying 1 A.

chapters.example: A 3 Ω resistor is connected across terminals A and B and is fed from a 12 V source through 6 Ω, with the 3 Ω itself forming the shunt to B. Find the Thevenin and Norton equivalents seen by a load across A and B, then find the load current for a 2 Ω load. Answers: V_th = 12 × 3/(6 + 3) = 4 V; R_th = 6 ∥ 3 = 2 Ω; I_N = 4/2 = 2 A in parallel with 2 Ω; with R_L = 2 Ω, I_L = 4/(2 + 2) = 1 A.
chapters.trap: Including the load resistance inside R_th, or killing a source the wrong way — a voltage source becomes a short, a current source becomes an open.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 1.4, 1.6 and 1.7 for reduction, equation solving and the idea of adding source responses.
chapters.leave: Choosing the load for maximum power to chapter 1.9; Thevenin equivalents of circuits with capacitors and inductors to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: A source delivers maximum power to a load when the load resistance equals the resistance seen looking back from the load, and that maximum is V_th²/(4R_th).
chapters.depth: Derive from P_L = I²R_L = V_th² R_L/(R_th + R_L)², differentiate with respect to R_L or complete the square, and get R_L = R_th. Then P_max = V_th²/(4R_th). Show the power curve: zero at both ends, peak at R_L = R_th. Work out the efficiency at that point: half the source power is lost in R_th, so efficiency is 50 percent, which is why power systems are not matched but audio and communication circuits are. Mention that R_L must be a resistance, that R_th may come from a Thevenin equivalent containing dependent sources, and that for a fixed R_L the transfer is best when R_th is small.

figure.aria: Load power plotted against load resistance, rising to a peak of 50 W at 2 Ω and falling away on either side of it.

chapters.example: A source has an open-circuit voltage V_th = 20 V and a Thevenin resistance R_th = 2 Ω. Find the load resistance for maximum power, that maximum power, and the efficiency there. Answers: R_L = R_th = 2 Ω; I = 20/4 = 5 A; P_max = 5² × 2 = 50 W, which also equals V_th²/(4R_th) = 400/8; total source power = 20 × 5 = 100 W, so efficiency is 50 percent.
chapters.trap: Reading the theorem as 'maximum efficiency' — at maximum power transfer half the source power is wasted in R_th, so it is the worst operating point for a power system.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.8 for the Thevenin equivalent from which V_th and R_th come.
chapters.leave: Impedance matching with reactances to Unit 2; matching transformers and machine loading to Unit 3.
